claims.text: Applying a conformal alumina coating by atomic layer deposition will improve the high-temperature oxygen resistance of a refractory high-entropy alloy.
The untreated refractory high-entropy alloy forms rapidly growing, non-protective oxide scales under high-temperature oxidizing conditions.
The proposed alumina coating is ultrathin, with a thickness of a few tens of nanometers.
The coating should provide oxidation protection during approximately 100 hours of exposure at 1000–1200 °C in air or a controlled oxygen atmosphere.
The preformed alumina layer acts as a barrier at the metal/oxide interface.
The ALD-deposited alumina layer limits oxygen ingress into the alloy.
The ALD-deposited alumina layer limits rapid outward diffusion of alloying elements.
Restricting oxygen ingress and elemental outward diffusion promotes formation of a slow-growing, adherent protective oxide scale.
Cracking and spallation of an oxide scale can accelerate oxidation or produce breakaway-like oxidation behavior.
The ultrathin coating does not alter the bulk properties of the refractory high-entropy alloy.
After 100 hours at 1000–1200 °C, the coated alloy will have significantly lower oxidation weight gain than the untreated alloy.
After 100 hours at 1000–1200 °C, the coated alloy will exhibit greater oxide-scale adherence and less spallation than the untreated alloy.
The improvement is expected only under oxidizing conditions at 1000–1200 °C and may not apply at lower temperatures or in non-oxidizing environments.
Coating uniformity and long-term thermal cycling can affect the magnitude of the oxidation improvement and scale integrity.
